takeaways: When the order of content changes its meaning, the order in code matches the order people should read it in.
Screen readers read the code order, not the layout. If the two disagree, people hear things in the wrong sequence.
It only matters where order changes meaning: steps, a price and what it is for, a question and its answer.
This is about reading order. Where keyboard focus goes next is 2.4.3.
failures: Columns that read across rows instead of down
A layout reordered visually so the code order no longer makes sense
Spaces or tabs used to fake columns of text
check: Number the content blocks on each frame in the order they should be read.
Compare that order with how the layers are stacked in your file.
In the build, use a screen reader or reader mode and listen for anything out of sequence.

quiz.question: Six setup steps are laid out in two columns: 1 to 3 on the left, 4 to 6 on the right. The build is in rows, so the code reads 1, 4, 2, 5, 3, 6. What do you annotate?
options: Nothing. Screen readers follow the visual layout
Only the tab order, since that is what developers set
The reading order, 1 to 6, so the code order matches the steps
quiz.why: Screen readers follow the code, so people would hear the steps jumbled. The steps are not interactive, so tab order does not fix it.

spec: Mark the reading order on frames where it is not simply top to bottom.
Flag any place where the visual order will differ from the code order, and say which one is right.
For responsive layouts, confirm the reading order still makes sense at each breakpoint.
review: If you read this aloud from top to bottom in code, does it still make sense?
Where does the layout move things away from where they belong in the story?
Which parts of this page have an order that matters?
tradeoff: Clever grid layouts can put things in a different place from the code. Keep visual moves small, or design the layout around the reading order so both agree.
system: Document the reading order for each pattern and layout template, so teams do not reinvent it frame by frame.
pitch: If the code order is wrong, a screen reader user hears step four before step two. The content is there, but it no longer makes sense.
